questions.question: Does acquisition capture everything downstream fact-extraction needs?
questions.finding: yes for this repository's real structure, via a full working-tree clone rather than selective fetch
questions.detail: clone_baseline() performs a real git clone --depth 1 of the entire working tree, so every file is reachable by any stage reading snapshot.root_path directly. RepositorySnapshotV1 itself stores only readme_path/readme_sha256, inventory_sha256 (aggregate), and package_roots -- license_path/community_paths are computed by file_inventory.scan() but not stored as named snapshot fields, only indirectly covered by inventory_sha256.

questions.question: Are README-only / monorepo / generated-source / LFS / submodule / missing-manifest conditions represented truthfully?
questions.finding: yes for this repository -- confirmed against real GitHub data, not inferred
questions.detail: Not README-only, not a monorepo, not generated-source, no LFS pointers, no submodules (confirmed via the real tree, 427 entries, not truncated). Manifest is legacy setup.py (no pyproject.toml); dependency_snapshot.py._python_snapshot() correctly returns applicable=False with an explicit not_applicable_reason rather than fabricating zero dependencies -- this module's own docstring cites a real prior incident (MT041) for exactly this failure mode.

questions.question: Does every consumer of Python dependency data represent a setup.py-only manifest as honestly as dependency_snapshot.py does?
questions.finding: no -- a second, parallel consumer silently returns [] with no gap flag for any non-pyproject.toml manifest
questions.detail: declared_python_runtime_dependencies() and declared_python_build_dependencies() guard on `manifest.name != "pyproject.toml"` and return a bare [] -- no error, no gap flag, no not_applicable_reason -- for any setup.py/setup.cfg-only Python repository. Independently re-verified by the coordinating session via direct grep of the file (not merely accepted from the subagent's quote): confirmed the exact guard text at both call sites. For THIS repository the result happens to be correct by coincidence (real setup.py has install_requires=[], confirmed via gh api contents/setup.py), so nothing is visibly wrong today for aspose-3d-foss/Aspose.3D-FOSS-for-Python specifically. The risk is structural: any other setup.py-based Python FOSS repo in the portfolio with a non-empty install_requires would hit this exact silent-[] path.
questions.smallest_repair_hypothesis: either delegate to dependency_snapshot.py's applicable/not_applicable_reason gate, or extend these two functions to read setup.py's install_requires (parsed, not executed) and only return [] with an explicit not_applicable_reason when truly no manifest is present -- not implemented in this read-only boundary
questions.regression_test_hypothesis: a setup.py-only fixture repo with a non-empty install_requires list, asserting the dependency-derived output is not silently []

questions.question: Is every snapshot input content-addressed, and is acquisition reproducible?
questions.finding: partially -- README is individually hashed, the rest of the tree only via one aggregate hash; the object is not byte-reproducible only because of an expected capture timestamp
questions.detail: inventory_sha256 = sha256(git ls-tree -r --full-tree HEAD), a single aggregate hash that transitively content-addresses every tracked file (any byte change anywhere flips it) but exposes no per-file breakdown. readme_sha256 is the only individually content-addressed file. captured_at (datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()) is the only field that keeps the serialized snapshot object from being byte-reproducible across two acquisitions at the same SHA -- an intentional capture timestamp, not a content field, so this is expected non-determinism, not a defect.
